completeScope: All 68 assigned physical PDF pages, not the entire book. Pages 1–172 are reviewed by other agents.
method: Sequential full reading of physical pages from private page extraction, bounded output without truncation. No raw source text is reproduced here.

points: Contrasts professed knowledge with actual action when old expectations and a new plan conflict.
Uses two opposite dog stories to challenge universal claims: fear of every dog after harm and trust in every dog after friendly contact both ignore variation.
Suggests observing expectations, thoughts and behavior rather than assuming a new statement has already changed a habit.
Discusses automatic skills, self-evaluation and alleged barriers to profit.
corrections: Beliefs possessing consciousness or physical conserved energy are author metaphors, not demonstrated mechanisms. Conservation of energy does not establish that beliefs cannot be forgotten or destroyed.
A favorable example does not establish that another similar case is safe. Neither dog story is a clinical exposure protocol or instruction to approach an animal.
Financial risk remains real after uncertainty is accepted. Calmness does not imply that loss or threat is impossible.
The drunk-driving analogy and claims of rare harm are unsupported and excluded.
Do not infer unconscious self-sabotage, childhood guilt or unworthiness from order-entry errors or a drawdown. First check recorded execution, method, costs, data and risk.

points: 193–201: mechanical/discretionary/intuitive stages; observe thoughts, words and actions; distinguish an error from a judgment of personal worth; larger position size amplifies the consequences of execution mistakes.
202–207: running example becomes a concrete goal, dated observations of distance/time/state and repeated redirection of attention. It illustrates practice structure, not a trading advantage.

207–212: seven stability principles concern identifying the setup, calculating and accepting risk, executing it, taking profits, monitoring errors and following principles. Exercise assumes an edge; belief alone is not its source.

212–216: choose one liquid instrument, specify exact entry, invalidation and exit variables; one execution timeframe, with another timeframe allowed as a predeclared directional filter. Do not invent discretionary conditions while the exercise is running.

217–219: split an illustrative linear position into three or four parts, take the first partial profit, identify a second target, move the remaining stop after that target; plan the final exit near a higher-timeframe level. The author's old tick distances and historical personal outcome frequencies are examples.

220–225: select a batch of 20 or more events, estimate its maximum planned exposure, reduce size or use a demonstration account if unaffordable; keep system variables fixed, record every eligible event and assess execution across the batch rather than changing the rule after each result.

226–229: repeated opinion questionnaire covers certainty, risk calculation, clear signals, drawdowns, personalizing the market, unplanned entries, fear of missing moves and views of success. It is not a validated diagnostic test or a measured profitability assessment.
corrections: The stages are the author's framework, not a certified progression; anecdotes do not prove intuition predicts future price.
The text's conscious belief energy, guaranteed change of identity and irreversible freedom from errors are not scientific mechanisms or promises the course adopts.
A profitable series or calm execution cannot establish positive expectancy. Market outcomes need not be independent or stationary, unlike the simplified casino comparison.

Twenty is the author's practical training batch, not a statistical proof threshold. Continuing every monetary attempt is never required after a safety stop, data failure or exhaustion of the declared budget; mark the batch interrupted and retain records.

At 217 the wording about a stop at 18 ticks is inconsistent with six ticks per contract; the following arithmetic shows 18 is total contract-ticks for three contracts, not price distance. After first +4 and two −6, total is −8 contract-ticks, a reduction of 10 from −18.

At 222, historical large-contract example is 3 contracts ×3 points ×250 per point=2250 total, ×20=45000. With a fivefold smaller multiplier, 450 is the three-contract total per attempt, not risk per each contract; per contract would be150, batch9000. No present instrument specification is inferred.
Break-even stop is not zero economic risk: fees, spread, gaps and slippage remain. The author explicitly allows a gap exception at218 despite guarantee language.
A target-to-stop ratio3:1 does not itself prove actual average win/loss3:1; partial closes change realized payoff, and costs raise the breakeven frequency.
A demo environment may differ in fills, liquidity, costs and emotions; it is useful practice but not identical to live execution. No account registration or deposit is required.
The running story is not an exercise prescription; fatigue/injury concerns should not be dismissed as excuses. No psychological diagnosis is made from an execution error.

laboratorySuggestions.name: One frozen rule across a batch
laboratorySuggestions.design: Before revealing future outcomes, freeze entry/skip, invalidation, exit, data source/timeframes, unit size, costs, per-attempt risk and batch/session stops. Present 20 hidden cases sequentially; capture the same fields each time, all eligible events and rule-based skips. Keep separate execution score and net outcome. Predefine interruption for budget/data/safety; no forced real trades. New rules get a new version and a fresh batch.
laboratorySuggestions.assessment: Successful execution can accompany a negative result; a profitable violation is still a violation. Twenty cases verify practice on that sample, not durable edge.

laboratorySuggestions.name: Three parts, different exits
laboratorySuggestions.design: Use a linear toy position: three units entered100, stop94; first target104, second108, last112. At first close +4, remaining original stops yield total−8. After second close +8, move last stop100: ordinary fill gives total+12; gap fill80 gives−8 before costs. Show units, realized result, remaining stop exposure and costs separately. This is not a fixed-payout binary contract.
laboratorySuggestions.assessment: Distinguish stop price distance6 from total risk18; closing one part reduces exposure but does not prove partial exit superiority or zero risk.

laboratorySuggestions.name: Expectation and counterexample
laboratorySuggestions.design: Record one absolute expectation and one observable fact before reveal; reveal a rule-compliant loss and a profitable violation, then rewrite only the expectation as a testable conditional. Preserve the initial record.
laboratorySuggestions.assessment: Do not convert emotional discomfort or confidence into market evidence or diagnose the learner.
